notes.meaning: Sanballat became very angry when he discovered that the Jews had actually begun rebuilding the city wall. He tried to hide his worry behind insults, mocking God's people in public. He hoped his sharp words would discourage the builders and stop the project before it gained momentum.

Sanballat spoke before his fellow leaders and the Samaritan army to stir up hatred against the Jews. He laughed at them as weak and asked if they thought a few sacrifices and burnt, crumbled stones could rebuild a fortress in a single day. He pointed out their real physical weakness while ignoring the power of the living God who was helping them.

Tobiah joined in the mockery by claiming that even a light, stepping fox could knock over their stone wall. Wild foxes often roamed through the ruins of Jerusalem, so he used that picture to say the repairs were flimsy and useless. His joke was meant to make the builders feel that their hard work was completely pointless.

Instead of arguing with the mockers, Nehemiah took the insult straight to God in prayer. He asked the Lord to hear their cries and make their enemies suffer the shame and exile they wished on Judah. Taking grief to God in prayer kept the people from acting out of personal revenge.

Nehemiah asked God not to overlook the sins of these enemies, because by insulting the builders they were really defying God Himself. In the Old Testament, calling for God's judgment against cruel oppressors was a plea for divine justice to protect God's name and people. He left the punishment entirely in God's hands rather than taking matters into his own.

The workers ignored the insults and closed all the gaps around the city until the wall reached half its planned height. The project moved forward quickly because the people threw their whole hearts into the work. When God gives His people unity and willingness, great tasks make rapid progress despite opposition.

Jerusalem was now completely surrounded by hostile neighbors from the north, south, east, and west. When these leaders saw that the gaps were closing and the walls were rising, their mockery turned into burning rage. They realized that a fortified Jerusalem would threaten their regional power and control.

These surrounding groups set aside their own differences to unite in a plot against Jerusalem. They planned to launch an armed raid to cause confusion and force the construction to halt. Whenever God's work moves forward, opposing forces often combine their efforts to hinder it.

Nehemiah met this deadly threat with both prayer and practical action. The people cried out to God for protection, and they also posted sentries around the clock to watch for an attack. True faith in God does not replace careful duty, but works hand in hand with wise precautions.

The people of Judah began to grow weary as the heavy labor dragged on. Piles of broken stone and debris still had to be hauled away, and the workers felt their strength slipping away. Weariness and discouragement often attack God's servants when a task is only half completed.

The enemies plotted a surprise attack, hoping to strike before the Jews could see them coming. Their goal was to kill the builders and put an end to the rebuilding once and for all. This secret plotting was intended to spread terror and paralyze the city with fear.

Jews living out in the border towns heard the enemies talking and rushed to Jerusalem to give repeated warnings. They told Nehemiah over and over that an ambush was being prepared from every direction. Their repeated alarms added fear to the fatigue the builders were already feeling.

Nehemiah placed armed guards behind the lowest and most exposed sections of the wall. He organized these defenders by family groups, armed with swords, spears, and bows, where the enemies could clearly see them. Standing alongside their own relatives gave the defenders extra courage to protect each other.

After inspecting the defenses, Nehemiah urged the leaders and the common people not to give in to fear. He reminded them of the awesome power of the Lord and challenged them to fight bravely for their families, wives, and homes. Remembering God's greatness gives people the courage to stand up against intimidating threats.

When the enemies realized their surprise plot had been uncovered and prepared for, they gave up the attack. Nehemiah gave all the credit to God for breaking up the enemy scheme. With the immediate danger gone, every worker went back to his post on the wall.

From that day on, Nehemiah divided his personal workforce into two shifts. One half worked on the wall while the other half stood guard in armor, holding weapons ready for combat. The city leaders stationed themselves behind the working families to give direction and support in case of danger.

Those who hauled heavy building supplies carried loads with one hand while keeping a weapon ready in the other. This showed that the workers stayed fully prepared for both labor and combat at every moment. Believers must continually work for the Lord while staying on guard against spiritual attacks.

The skilled stone masons needed both hands to set the stones, so each one kept a sword strapped to his belt while he worked. Meanwhile, a trumpeter stayed right beside Nehemiah so an alarm could be sounded instantly. Everyone remained ready to drop their tools and fight at a moment's notice.

Nehemiah explained to the nobles, leaders, and people that the wall was very long and the workers were scattered far apart. This wide distance made small groups vulnerable to being overrun if an enemy struck one spot. Recognizing their vulnerability helped them see the need for clear communication and quick teamwork.

Nehemiah commanded the people to run toward the sound of the trumpet whenever it blew, gathering together for defense. He encouraged them with the promise that God Himself would fight on their side. Trusting God's help gave them the confidence to stand together against superior numbers.

The builders kept up the hard work from early dawn until the night stars came out, while half the guard held spears ready for battle. They poured long, exhausting hours into the project without complaining. Their dedication showed their deep desire to see the city of God restored and secure.

Nehemiah ordered all the workers and their helpers from the countryside to sleep inside Jerusalem instead of walking home each evening. This kept the workforce together so they could guard the city at night and rebuild it during the day. It also protected the workers from being ambushed out in their undefended villages.

Nehemiah, his close relatives, his servants, and his bodyguard set an example by never taking off their clothes to sleep. They stayed dressed and kept their weapons in hand around the clock, even when fetching water. True leaders share the hardships of those they lead and remain constantly alert.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translation reads the end of this verse as saying that the men took off their clothes only when they washed or bathed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars generally understand the difficult Hebrew phrase to mean that each man kept his weapon at his right hand, even when going to the water.
